title: Fear and dread
hookLine: alone in the forest at night, he met fear in whatever posture it found him (MN 4)
carry: face it where it finds you

lines: A SHRINE IN A GROVE AT NIGHT.
cards: Night in an old Indian forest. No light anywhere but the moon, if that. A man sits alone at a shrine in a grove, the kind of place people avoid after dark.
A twig snaps. Leaves rustle. Something moves in the dark.
And his heart pounds: here it comes, the fear, the dread. This comes from his own telling, years later. It's the Buddha, before his awakening, describing nights he chose on purpose.

teach.b: MN 4, the Bhayabherava. A brahmin named Janussoni tells the Buddha: forest life must be hard for a monk; the mind of someone without concentration would be swept away. Yes, says the Buddha; I thought so too, before.
Then he explains two things. First, conduct. People who go into the forest with harmful actions, speech or ways of living, with greed or ill will, call up fear and dread for themselves.
He looked at himself, found his conduct clean, and that gave him great confidence in the wilderness. Second, the fear came anyway.
On the special nights of the moon's fortnight, he went to the frightening places: shrines in parks and woods, under great trees.

teach.h: A DEER, A PEACOCK, THE WIND.
teach.b: A deer would come by. A peacock would knock down a twig. The wind would stir the leaves.
And he'd think: here it comes, the fear and dread. So he made a resolve. Why keep waiting for fear?
Why not subdue it in whatever posture it finds me? If it came while he walked, he kept walking until it passed. If he stood, he stood.
If he sat, he stayed sitting. If he was lying down, he didn't get up. He never ran to a better position first.

teach.h: HE NEVER SAYS HE WASN'T AFRAID.
teach.b: And notice what he never says: that he wasn't afraid.

teach.h: FACE IT WHERE IT FINDS YOU.
teach.b: He met it where it found him. So the week closes: the path walked whole, the Middle-Length Sayings opened, the root of all things, the taints, wise attention, the heirs, and the forest at night.

how: In Thai and other forest traditions, monks have long practiced in wild and frightening places, including charnel grounds, as a way of meeting fear directly; many teachers also stress keeping precepts as a ground of confidence.

o: the courage of someone who feels no fear
a monk's vow to live alone in the forest
fear and dread, the terror of lonely places

p: says forest life must be hard

s: the Buddha says he never felt fear in the forest
fear and dread came; he met them where they found him.
he chose frightening places on purpose
shrines in parks and woods, on special nights of the fortnight.
he waited until he was sitting down before facing fear
walking, standing, sitting or lying, he stayed in that posture until it passed.

games.q: you're walking alone in a dark grove and fear arrives. what did the Buddha-to-be do, in MN 4?
o: sat down to meditate on it
kept walking until the fear was subdued
games.why: he kept walking. he didn't stand, sit or lie down until he'd subdued it. no better position first.

practice: Choose a small fear, not the biggest one, an email you haven't opened, a conversation you've been avoiding, and notice where it lands in the body.
Then do what the text describes: stay in the posture it finds you, no shifting, no reaching for your phone. Breathe with it until it changes, even a little.

wordCard.voice: Bhaya-bherava, fear and dread. The terror of lonely places, met by the Buddha in whatever posture it found him.

orig.note: Pali bhaya-bherava: fear and dread, the terror of wild places; the name of MN 4.

carryVoice: Your line: face it where it finds you. The fear can come along; you don't have to move. That's the week; see you tomorrow.
